Nephrotoxicity has been associated with high plasma concentrations of fluoride during anaesthesia with fluorine-containing anaesthetics such as methoxyflurane (p.1789). Elevated fluoride ion concentrations have also been noted in the plasma of patients receiving enflurane or isoflurane, although no clinical effect on renal function was found (see Ef- fects on the Kidneys, p.1782 and Metabolism, p.1786). Fluorosis. Discussions of chronic fluorosis.1-5 In a 1994 report, WHO considered that in temperate climates, teeth seemed not to be affected if fluoride concentrations in drinking water were not greatly above 1 ppm; fluorosis affecting bone had not been de- tected at concentrations of 4 to 8 ppm in temperate regions, al- though it could occur at concentrations of more than 6 ppm in tropical areas.6 However, a later systematic review7 of the effects of water fluoridation, which included 214 studies worldwide, considered that at a concentration of 1 ppm, an estimated 12.5% of exposed people would develop sufficient fluorosis of their teeth to cause aesthetic concern. Swallowing of fluoridated toothpaste by young children has been implicated as a risk factor for fluorosis.4,8 Higher concentrations of fluoride in toothpaste have been associated with less caries, but with higher levels of fluorosis,9 and toothpastes with lower concentrations of fluoride have been recommended for use in children.8,9 The use of infant formula feeds reconstituted with fluoridated water may result in ingestion of large amounts of fluoride5 and subsequent fluoro- sis;3 bottled water may also contain fluoride.5 Skeletal fluorosis associated with excess tea consumption has also been reported (see Effects on Bones and Joints, above). 1.
